claim: Various members of the OSCA and TMEM63 family of proteins from plants, flies, and mammals confer mechanosensitivity to naïve cells.
source: Here, we show that various members of the OSCA and TMEM63 family of proteins from plants, flies, and mammals confer mechanosensitivity to naïve cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing mechanically activated currents in cells expressing OSCA and TMEM63 proteins from different species.

claim: OSCA1.2 is an inherently mechanosensitive, pore-forming ion channel.
source: We conclusively demonstrate that OSCA1.2, one of the Arabidopsis thaliana OSCA proteins, is an inherently mechanosensitive, pore-forming ion channel.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from proteoliposome reconstitution experiments showing stretch-activated currents from purified OSCA1.2 protein.

claim: OSCA/TMEM63 proteins are the largest family of MA ion channels identified and are conserved across eukaryotes.
source: Our results suggest that OSCA/TMEM63 proteins are the largest family of MA ion channels identified, and are conserved across eukaryotes.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates mechanosensitivity in multiple OSCA and TMEM63 family members from plants, flies, and mammals, and notes that Arabidopsis thaliana alone has 15 OSCA members.

claim: PIEZO family of mechanically activated ion channels mediate touch sensation and vascular development in mammals.
source: In mammals, some mechanosensory processes such as touch sensation and vascular development are mediated by the PIEZO family of mechanically activated (MA) ion channels (Coste et al., 2010; Coste et al., 2012; Murthy et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: The mechanotransduction complex in hair cells includes TMC1 as the pore-forming ion channel and comprises TMHS and TMIE.
source: For hearing, the mechanotransduction complex in hair cells includes TMC1 as the pore-forming ion channel, but also comprises of TMHS and TMIE (Ballesteros et al., 2018; Pan et al., 2018; Qiu and Müller, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: MSL8 is involved in pollen hydration in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Homologues of the bacterial MA channel MscS-Like (MSLs) exist in plants, and MSL8 is shown to be involved in pollen hydration in Arabidopsis thaliana (Cox et al., 2015; Hamilton et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Hyperosmolarity-evoked intracellular calcium increase is dependent on OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 genes in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Beyond MSLs, hyperosmolarity-evoked intracellular calcium increase is shown to be dependent on the genes OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 in Arabidopsis thaliana (Hou et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Hyperosmolarity-evoked whole-cell currents recorded from OSCA1.1- or OSCA1.2-expressing cells were only modestly larger than baseline currents.
source: In contrast to published reports (Hou et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2014), we find that hyperosmolarity-evoked whole-cell currents recorded from OSCA1.1- or OSCA1.2-expressing cells were only modestly larger than baseline currents (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MA whole-cell currents recorded from cells transfected with OSCA1.1 or OSCA1.2 were 10- and 100-fold larger than their hyperosmolarity-activated currents, respectively.
source: Surprisingly, MA whole-cell currents recorded from cells transfected with OSCA1.1 or OSCA1.2 were 10- and 100-fold larger than their hyperosmolarity-activated currents, respectively (Figure 1A,B vs. Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing mechanically activated and hyperosmolarity-activated currents shown in Figure 1.

claim: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 whole-cell MA currents had an apparent activation threshold of 8.6 ± 0.9 µm and 6.3 ± 0.7 µm, respectively.
source: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 whole-cell MA currents had an apparent activation threshold of 8.6 ± 0.9 µm and 6.3 ± 0.7 µm, and inactivated (channel closure in continued presence of stimulus) with a time constant of 10.0 ± 1.3 ms and 10.4 ± 1.7 ms, respectively (Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 whole-cell MA currents inactivated with a time constant of 10.0 ± 1.3 ms and 10.4 ± 1.7 ms, respectively.
source: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 whole-cell MA currents had an apparent activation threshold of 8.6 ± 0.9 µm and 6.3 ± 0.7 µm, and inactivated (channel closure in continued presence of stimulus) with a time constant of 10.0 ± 1.3 ms and 10.4 ± 1.7 ms, respectively (Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: Robust macroscopic stretch-activated currents were recorded from cells transfected with OSCA1.1 or OSCA1.2 but not from mock-transfected cells.
source: Similarly, robust macroscopic stretch-activated currents were recorded from cells transfected with OSCA1.1 or OSCA1.2 but not from mock-transfected cells (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Stretch-activated currents from OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 were reversible and inactivated with a time constant of 24 ± 3.4 ms and 24.6 ± 4.8 ms, respectively.
source: Stretch-activated currents from OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 were reversible and inactivated with a time constant of 24 ± 3.4 ms and 24.6 ± 4.8 ms, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The pressure required for half-maximal activation (P50) of OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 was -58.5 ± 3.7 mmHg and -54.5 ± 2.2 mmHg, respectively.
source: The pressure required for half-maximal activation (P50) of OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 was -58.5 ± 3.7 mmHg and -54.5 ± 2.2 mmHg, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mouse PIEZO1 has a threshold of -24 ± 3.6 mmHg.
source: These values are higher than mouse PIEZO1 which has a threshold of -24 ± 3.6 mmHg (Coste et al., 2010; Coste et al., 2015) (Figure 1E and Table 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications and data shown in Figure 1E and Table 1.

claim: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 evoke high-threshold MA currents in HEK-P1KO cells.
source: These values are higher than mouse PIEZO1 which has a threshold of -24 ± 3.6 mmHg (Coste et al., 2010; Coste et al., 2015) (Figure 1E and Table 1), demonstrating that at least in HEK-P1KO cells these proteins evoke high-threshold MA currents.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with published values.

claim: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 are involved in mechanotransduction.
source: These results suggest that OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 are involved in mechanotransduction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing mechanically activated currents.

claim: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 belong to a family of genes that include 15 members across four clades in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 belong to a family of genes that include 15 members across four clades (Hou et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2014) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 share 85% sequence identity.
source: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 share 85% sequence identity, while other family members within the same clade are more divergent (50 – 70%).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Other OSCA family members within the same clade are more divergent (50 – 70% identity).
source: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 share 85% sequence identity, while other family members within the same clade are more divergent (50 – 70%).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genes within Clade 2 have about 30% identity to Clade 1.
source: Genes within Clade 2 have about 30% identity to Clade 1, and Clade 3 and 4 share the least homology with Clade 1 (Figure 2A and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2A and Table 2.

claim: Clade 3 and 4 share the least homology with Clade 1.
source: Genes within Clade 2 have about 30% identity to Clade 1, and Clade 3 and 4 share the least homology with Clade 1 (Figure 2A and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2A and Table 2.

claim: Mechanical indentation of cells expressing OSCA1.8, OSCA2.3, OSCA3.1, or OSCA4.1 did not elicit MA currents in the whole-cell patch clamp mode.
source: In the whole-cell patch clamp mode, mechanical indentation of cells expressing OSCA1.8, OSCA2.3, OSCA3.1, or OSCA4.1 did not elicit MA currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Distinct stretch-activated currents were recorded from cells expressing OSCA1.8, OSCA2.3, or OSCA3.1, but not OSCA4.1.
source: Remarkably, however, distinct stretch-activated currents were recorded from cell expressing OSCA1.8, OSCA2.3, or OSCA3.1, but not OSCA4.1 (Figure 2B,C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C and Table 1.

claim: The three mechanosensitive OSCA proteins (OSCA1.8, OSCA2.3, OSCA3.1) had disparate gating kinetics, with different inactivation time constants.
source: The three mechanosensitive OSCA proteins had disparate gating kinetics, with different inactivation time constants (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The pressure of half-maximal activation was comparable among all the mechanosensitive OSCA proteins.
source: While the pressure of half-maximal activation was comparable among all the mechanosensitive OSCA proteins (Figure 2D), the most striking feature was the diversity in their single-channel conductance (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The most striking feature among mechanosensitive OSCA proteins was the diversity in their single-channel conductance.
source: While the pressure of half-maximal activation was comparable among all the mechanosensitive OSCA proteins (Figure 2D), the most striking feature was the diversity in their single-channel conductance (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: OSCA1.8 channel conductance was approximately four-fold smaller than OSCA1.1.
source: OSCA1.8 and OSCA3.1 channel conductance was approximately four- and six-fold smaller than OSCA1.1, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing single-channel conductances.

claim: OSCA3.1 channel conductance was approximately six-fold smaller than OSCA1.1.
source: OSCA1.8 and OSCA3.1 channel conductance was approximately four- and six-fold smaller than OSCA1.1, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing single-channel conductances.

claim: Single-channel amplitude of OSCA2.3 stretch-activated currents were in the sub-picoampere range and unresolvable.
source: Furthermore, single-channel amplitude of OSCA2.3 stretch-activated currents were in the sub-picoampere range and unresolvable, which could explain the relatively smaller maximal current responses (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: OSCAs are a family of MA ion channels with unique biophysical properties.
source: These results provide evidence that OSCAs are a family of MA ion channels with unique biophysical properties.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing diverse biophysical properties among OSCA family members.

claim: Different members of the OSCA family have differential responses to the two types of mechanical stimulation (indentation vs. stretch).
source: Intriguingly, the different members of the OSCA family have differential responses to the two types of mechanical stimulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that some OSCA members respond to stretch but not indentation.

claim: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 had a high threshold (8 µm) compared to mouse PIEZO1 (4 – 5 µm).
source: It is noteworthy that OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 which were the only channels activated by membrane indentation, had a high threshold (8 µm) compared to mouse PIEZO1 (4 – 5 µm) (Dubin et al., 2017) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous publication.

claim: HEK-P1KO cells often break near 10 – 12 µm of indentation.
source: Perhaps other OSCA channels have a much higher threshold, technically limiting us from recording reliable MA currents, since HEK-P1KO cells often break near 10 – 12 µm of indentation.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations during electrophysiology recordings.

claim: Mechanical indentation and membrane stretch deliver biophysically-distinct forces to the membrane.
source: Alternatively, mechanical indentation and membrane stretch deliver biophysically-distinct forces to the membrane and the different proteins might be tuned to the unique type of force applied.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the differential responses observed.

claim: Under physiological ionic conditions, OSCA1.1- and OSCA1.2-dependent stretch-activated currents had single-channel conductance of 184 ± 4 pS and 122 ± 3 pS, respectively.
source: Under physiological ionic conditions, OSCA1.1- and OSCA1.2-dependent stretch-activated currents had single-channel conductance of 184 ± 4 pS and 122 ± 3 pS, respectively (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: The single-channel conductance values for OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 are larger than what was previously reported.
source: We note that these values are larger than what was previously reported (Yuan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim compares current findings with a previous publication.

claim: The single-channel conductance described in Yuan et al., 2014 was measured in the absence of a stimulus, and might not be strictly OSCA-dependent.
source: Unlike our measurements, the single-channel conductance described in Yuan et al., 2014 was measured in the absence of a stimulus, and might not be strictly OSCA-dependent.
evidence: The claim is based on methodological differences between studies and inference about the nature of the measurements.

claim: Stretch-activated single-channel current traces from OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 revealed a single sub-conductance state, which was half the amplitude of the full open state.
source: Interestingly, stretch-activated single-channel current traces from either protein revealed a single sub-conductance state, which was half the amplitude of the full open state (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sub-conductance states are a hallmark of many ion channels and are indicative of concerted gating of multiple pores from the same channel, or of changes within a single pore.
source: Sub-conductance states are a hallmark of many ion channels and are indicative of concerted gating of multiple pores from the same channel, or of changes within a single pore (Dani and Fox, 1991; Hartzell and Whitlock, 2016; Miller, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: The presence of a single intermediate state in OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 could be suggestive of two cooperative subunits.
source: The presence of a single intermediate state in OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 could be suggestive of two cooperative subunits.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed sub-conductance states.

claim: The cryo-EM structures of OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 reveal a pore within each subunit of a dimeric channel.
source: Indeed, this suggestion is confirmed by the cryo-EM structures of OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2, which reveal a pore within each subunit of a dimeric channel (Jojoa Cruz et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 evoked non-selective cation currents with some chloride permeability (OSCA1.1: PCl/PNa = 0.21 ± 0.06; OSCA1.2: PCl/PNa = 0.17 ± 0.01).
source: Characterization of the stretch-activated currents in asymmetrical NaCl solutions revealed that OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 evoked non-selective cation currents with some chloride permeability (OSCA1.1: PCl/PNa = 0.21 ± 0.06; OSCA1.2: PCl/PNa = 0.17 ± 0.01) (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Gadolinium inhibited OSCA1.1- and OSCA1.2-induced stretch-activated currents.
source: In addition, gadolinium, a generic MA cation channel blocker, inhibited OSCA1.1- and OSCA1.2-induced stretch-activated currents (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 induce MA non-selective cation currents.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 induce MA non-selective cation currents.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on ion selectivity and gadolinium inhibition.

claim: Purified OSCA1.2-EGFP appears as a single protein band on a denaturing gel, indicating the absence of other associated proteins.
source: Purified OSCA1.2-EGFP (117 kDa) appears as a single protein band on a denaturing gel, indicating the absence of other associated proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MscL-like stretch-induced channel activity was observed in seven out of eight excised patches from liposomes reconstituted with E. coli MscL.
source: We observed MscL-like stretch-induced channel activity in seven out of eight excised patches (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–D.

claim: The stretch-activated single-channel currents from E. coli MscL had a conductance of 3340 ± 180 pS (N = 6), which is in accordance with previous reports.
source: The stretch-activated single-channel currents had a conductance of 3340 ± 180 pS (N = 6), which is in accordance with previous reports (Kloda and Martinac, 2002) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements and citation to previous publication.

claim: Applying negative pipette-pressure in the range of 0 to 50 mmHg to patches excised from liposomes reconstituted with OSCA1.2-EGFP protein induced robust macroscopic currents.
source: Remarkably, applying negative pipette-pressure in the range of 0 to 50 mmHg to patches excised from liposomes reconstituted with OSCA1.2-EGFP protein also induced robust macroscopic currents (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Applying negative pressure (as high 100 to 120 mmHg) to patches excised from empty liposomes did not change the baseline current.
source: Applying negative pressure (as high 100 to 120 mmHg) to patches excised from empty liposomes did not change the baseline current.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental control data.

claim: The stretch-activated currents from OSCA1.2 in proteoliposomes exhibited sub-conductance states and were voltage-dependent.
source: At the single-channel level, the stretch-activated currents exhibited sub-conductance states, were voltage-dependent, and had a conductance of 346 ± 13 pS in 200 mM KCl solution, which matched the single-channel conductance measured from OSCA1.2-expressing cells (304 ± 9 pS) under the same ionic concentration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3G,H.

claim: OSCA1.2 in proteoliposomes had a conductance of 346 ± 13 pS in 200 mM KCl solution, which matched the single-channel conductance measured from OSCA1.2-expressing cells (304 ± 9 pS) under the same ionic concentration.
source: At the single-channel level, the stretch-activated currents exhibited sub-conductance states, were voltage-dependent, and had a conductance of 346 ± 13 pS in 200 mM KCl solution, which matched the single-channel conductance measured from OSCA1.2-expressing cells (304 ± 9 pS) under the same ionic concentration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements comparing proteoliposomes and cells.

claim: OSCA1.2, like other bona-fide MA ion channels such as MscL, TREK and TRAAK, and PIEZO1, is directly gated by changes in membrane tension, and requires no additional cellular components for activation.
source: These results demonstrate that OSCA1.2, like other bona-fide MA ion channels such as MscL, TREK and TRAAK, and PIEZO1, is directly gated by changes in membrane tension, and requires no additional cellular components for activation (Anishkin et al., 2014; Brohawn et al., 2014; Häse et al., 1995; Syeda et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from proteoliposome reconstitution and citations to previous publications.

claim: OSCA1.2 encodes a pore-forming subunit and is inherently mechanosensitive.
source: This represents conclusive evidence that OSCA1.2 encodes a pore-forming subunit and is inherently mechanosensitive (Jojoa Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the proteoliposome reconstitution experiments and structural studies.

claim: TMEM63 family of proteins are the closest homologues of OSCAs.
source: Phylogenetic analysis and previous studies have identified the TMEM63 family of proteins as the closest homologues of OSCAs (Hou et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2014) (Figure 4A and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations to previous publications.

claim: Mechanical stimulation of cells expressing DmTMEM63, MmTMEM63A, MmTMEM63B, MmTMEM63C, or HsTMEM63A did not elicit MA currents in the whole-cell patch clamp mode.
source: In the whole-cell patch clamp mode, mechanical stimulation of cells expressing DmTMEM63, MmTMEM63A, MmTMEM63B, MmTMEM63C, or HsTMEM63A did not elicit MA currents (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: DmTMEM63, MmTMEM63A, MmTMEM63B, and HsTMEM63A (with the exception of MmTMEM63C) induced stretch-activated currents when expressed in naïve cells.
source: However, these clones (with the exception of MmTMEM63C) induced stretch-activated currents when expressed in naïve cells (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Mammalian TMEM63C is divergent from TMEM63A and TMEM63B.
source: The phylogenetic tree illustrates that mammalian TMEM63C is divergent from TMEM63A and TMEM63B (Figure 4A), which may explain its lack of mechanosensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: P50 values for the TMEM63-induced stretch-activated currents were in the range of -60 to -80 mmHg.
source: P50 values for the TMEM63-induced stretch-activated currents were in the range of -60 to -80 mmHg, suggesting that like OSCAs, these proteins elicit high-threshold MA currents in HEK-P1KO cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TMEM63 proteins elicit high-threshold MA currents in HEK-P1KO cells.
source: P50 values for the TMEM63-induced stretch-activated currents were in the range of -60 to -80 mmHg, suggesting that like OSCAs, these proteins elicit high-threshold MA currents in HEK-P1KO cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the P50 values measured experimentally.

claim: The stretch-activated single-channel currents induced by DmTMEM63 or the mammalian TMEM63s are in the sub-picoampere range and were unresolvable, similar to OSCA2.3.
source: The stretch-activated single-channel currents induced by either DmTMEM63 or the mammalian TMEM63s are in the sub-picoampere range and were unresolvable, similar to OSCA2.3 (Figure 4B vs. Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations comparing data in Figure 4B and Figure 2B.

claim: MA currents induced by the TMEM63 family members had unique gating properties with several fold slower activation and inactivation kinetics compared to plant OSCAs.
source: However, compared to plant OSCAs, MA currents induced by the TMEM63 family members had unique gating properties with several fold slower activation and inactivation kinetics (Figure 4D and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claim: MmTMEM63A stretch-activated currents are non-selective cationic.
source: MmTMEM63A stretch-activated currents are non-selective cationic, and gadolinium inhibits MmTMEM63A-induced MA currents by 75% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gadolinium inhibits MmTMEM63A-induced MA currents by 75%.
source: MmTMEM63A stretch-activated currents are non-selective cationic, and gadolinium inhibits MmTMEM63A-induced MA currents by 75% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: MmTMEM63A is expressed at the membrane.
source: At least MmTMEM63A is expressed at the membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), therefore trafficking issues cannot account for the relatively small stretch-activated macroscopic currents.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Orthologues of OSCAs induce stretch-activated currents when overexpressed in naïve cells.
source: Nonetheless, these results demonstrate that orthologues of OSCAs also induce stretch-activated currents when overexpressed in naïve cells, and that mechanosensitivity is conserved across the various members in the OSCA/TMEM63 family.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on TMEM63 proteins.

claim: Mechanosensitivity is conserved across the various members in the OSCA/TMEM63 family.
source: Nonetheless, these results demonstrate that orthologues of OSCAs also induce stretch-activated currents when overexpressed in naïve cells, and that mechanosensitivity is conserved across the various members in the OSCA/TMEM63 family.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing mechanosensitivity in OSCA and TMEM63 proteins from different species.

claim: Transfection of various members of the OSCA/TMEM63 family from plants, flies, and mammals give rise to robust MA currents.
source: We provide evidence that members of OSCA family are bona-fide, pore-forming mechanosensitive ion channels: (1) transfection of various members of the family from plants, flies, and mammals give rise to robust MA currents.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing MA currents in cells expressing OSCA/TMEM63 proteins.

claim: Single-channel conductance of individual OSCAs are quite distinct, arguing that the OSCAs contribute to pore properties of these currents.
source: Importantly, single-channel conductance of individual OSCAs are quite distinct, arguing that the OSCAs contribute to pore properties of these currents.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the diversity of single-channel conductances observed.

claim: OSCA1.2 is an inherently mechanosensitive ion channel in the absence of other proteins.
source: (2) We directly show in vitro (proteoliposomes) that OSCA1.2 is an inherently mechanosensitive ion channel in the absence of other proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteoliposome reconstitution experiments.

claim: The high-resolution structure of OSCA1.2 demonstrates that this protein has similar architecture to the TMEM16 family of ion channels.
source: (3) The accompanying paper describes the high-resolution structure of OSCA1.2 (Jojoa Cruz et al., 2018), and demonstrates that this protein has similar architecture to the TMEM16 family of ion channels (Whitlock and Hartzell, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a structural study.

claim: Structure-guided mutagenesis verifies that a residue within the putative pore-forming region contributes to single-channel conductance.
source: Furthermore, structure-guided mutagenesis verifies that a residue within the putative pore-forming region contributes to single-channel conductance (Jojoa Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a mutagenesis study.

claim: With 15 different members present just in Arabidopsis thaliana (5/6 members tested were mechanosensitive), OSCA/TMEM63 proteins potentially represent the largest family of mechanosensitive ion channels known to date.
source: Therefore, with 15 different members present just in Arabidopsis thaliana (5/6 members we tested were mechanosensitive), OSCA/TMEM63 proteins potentially represent the largest family of mechanosensitive ion channels known to date.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the number of family members and the proportion found to be mechanosensitive.

claim: No other eukaryotic ion channels are conserved from plants to humans.
source: Although other eukaryotic ion channels have been previously described, none are conserved from plants to humans.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of ion channel families across species.

claim: PIEZOs are present in plants and unicellular organisms.
source: PIEZOs are also present in plants and unicellular organisms; however, evidence that they are mechanosensitive in these species is still lacking.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of PIEZO distribution across species.

claim: Evidence that PIEZOs are mechanosensitive in plants and unicellular organisms is still lacking.
source: PIEZOs are also present in plants and unicellular organisms; however, evidence that they are mechanosensitive in these species is still lacking.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of published evidence.

claim: The existence of 15 members of OSCAs in Arabidopsis thaliana raises the possibility that there might be redundancy.
source: The existence of 15 members of OSCAs in Arabidopsis thaliana raises the possibility that there might be redundancy, and will make it a challenge to assign function to these proteins individually.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the implications of having multiple family members.

claim: Under hyperosmotic stress, mutant OSCA1.1 plants had stunted leaf and root growth.
source: However, Yuan et al., 2014reported that under hyperosmotic stress, mutant OSCA1.1 plants had stunted leaf and root growth (Yuan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication.

claim: The phenotypes of mutant OSCA1.1 plants could be a consequence of impaired mechanotransduction.
source: These phenotypes could indeed be a consequence of impaired mechanotransduction.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed phenotypes.

claim: Expression profile of mouse TMEM63A suggests expression in tissues that experience mechanical forces such as kidney and stomach.
source: Expression profile of mouse TMEM63A in public databases (BioGPS.org) suggests expression in tissues that experience mechanical forces such as kidney and stomach, while TMEM63B is high in the nervous system (including dorsal root ganglia) as well as in the heart, skeletal muscle, and stomach.
evidence: The claim is based on publicly available expression data.

claim: Mouse TMEM63B is highly expressed in the nervous system (including dorsal root ganglia) as well as in the heart, skeletal muscle, and stomach.
source: Expression profile of mouse TMEM63A in public databases (BioGPS.org) suggests expression in tissues that experience mechanical forces such as kidney and stomach, while TMEM63B is high in the nervous system (including dorsal root ganglia) as well as in the heart, skeletal muscle, and stomach.
evidence: The claim is based on publicly available expression data.

claim: Mechanotransduction is crucial for many biological processes in plants and animals.
source: Mechanotransduction, the conversion of mechanical cues into biochemical signals, is crucial for many biological processes in plants and animals (Arnadóttir and Chalfie, 2010; Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: The impact of gravity or soil properties on root development, wind on stem growth, and turgor pressure on plant-cell size and shape are proposed to involve activation of MA ion channels.
source: In plants, the impact of gravity or soil properties on root development, wind on stem growth, and turgor pressure on plant-cell size and shape are proposed to involve activation of MA ion channels (Hamant, 2013; Hamant and Haswell, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: The activation mechanism for OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 proteins and whether they encode a pore-forming ion channel remained unknown prior to this study.
source: Beyond MSLs, hyperosmolarity-evoked intracellular calcium increase is shown to be dependent on the genes OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 in Arabidopsis thaliana (Hou et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2014); however, the activation mechanism for these proteins and whether they encode a pore-forming ion channel remains unknown.
evidence: The claim describes the state of knowledge before the current study.

claim: Gadolinium blocks OSCA1.1 maximal current responses by 80%.
source: Gd3+ blocks OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 maximal current responses by 80% and 72%, respectively (**p=0.0023, Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Gadolinium blocks OSCA1.2 maximal current responses by 72%.
source: Gd3+ blocks OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 maximal current responses by 80% and 72%, respectively (**p=0.0023, Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The modest hyperosmolarity-induced currents might be due to osmotic shock causing cell shrinking, and affecting membrane tension.
source: We next explored the possibility that OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 are mechanosensitive, and that the modest hyperosmolarity-induced currents might be due to osmotic shock causing cell shrinking, and affecting membrane tension (Sachs, 2010).
